# Project objective

In this part of the project, you will build and program a simulated robot cell
in Visual Components (VC) and then coordinate it with a PLC program running in
CODESYS Control Win SL. The cell transports a raw part to a robot, loads it into
a CNC mill, waits for machining, unloads it, and returns the finished part to a
conveyor.

This page guides you through the work in the intended order, from assembling
and testing the VC-only cell to connecting and commissioning the
PLC-controlled version. Use it as a working tutorial: later steps build on the
checks completed in the earlier steps.

The work is divided into two stages:

1. Build and program a complete working cell using internal VC signals.
2. Transfer overall cell coordination to a PLC connected through OPC UA.

Do not begin with the PLC connection. First establish that the robot poses,
motions, gripper, CNC model, and complete material flow work inside VC. This
gives you a known-working plant before communication and distributed control
are introduced.

By completing the project, you should be able to:

- configure a robot, gripper, conveyor, sensor, and process machine in VC,
- divide a robot task into meaningful reusable subroutines,
- define a clear control boundary between a PLC and robot controller,
- design two controllers that coordinate through a command handshake,
- connect CODESYS and VC using OPC UA, and
- commission the system incrementally rather than debugging everything at once.

# Required cell behavior

The completed system shall repeat the following material flow:

1. Transport a raw part to the robot pickup position.
2. Stop the part and conveyor at the pickup position.
3. Pick the part and load it into the CNC mill.
4. Close the CNC door and start machining.
5. Confirm that machining starts and wait until it finishes.
6. Open the door and unload the finished part.
7. Place the part on the outgoing conveyor.
8. Return the robot to its home pose and prepare for the next part.

The first version is controlled by the robot program inside VC. In the final
version, the PLC controls the overall sequence while the robot executes
requested motion operations.

# Build the simulated cell

## Organize the project with sublayouts {#sec-cell-sublayouts}

Build the robot cell in the same VC file as the completed conveyor system,
but do not connect the two systems yet. Begin from the conveyor checkpoint and
keep its saved copy unchanged as a tested backup.
Place the new robot cell some distance away from the conveyor system, with
enough empty space that the two material flows remain clearly separate during
development.

The [conveyor-system instructions](conveyor.qmd#sec-conveyor-sublayout) create a
`Conveyor system` sublayout. Confirm that the completed conveyor components are
assigned to it, then create a second sublayout named `Robot cell`. Components
for the new cell are moved into this second sublayout after their initial
placement.

The roles of the Cell Graph, components, and sublayouts are introduced in
[Layouts and components](visual_components.qmd#sec-vc-layouts-components).
This structure keeps the complete system in one simulation while making each
section easier to select, move, copy, and inspect. The linked section also
contains the relevant VC Academy lesson.
Sublayout visibility is an organizational aid; hiding a sublayout does not
replace disconnecting or stopping components when you want to test only one
part of the system.

## Design the robot cell

Start with the Simple Robot Pedestal and the KUKA robot. Place the pedestal
in the 3D world and position the robot on top; you can use the attach tool to be able to move them together. The height of the pedestal can be adjusted as needed, and it is part of the cell design:
it determines whether the robot can approach the conveyor and CNC at useful
joint configurations, not only whether the TCP can reach them at all.

Next, add a short incoming conveyor and place a Conveyor Sensor close to its
downstream end. This sensor defines the repeatable pickup location. Copy and
paste the Advanced Feeder that is already configured in the conveyor system,
and configure only this copy to generate grey cylinders. Keep the original
mixed feeder unchanged in the `Conveyor system` sublayout. The temporary feeder
provides test parts immediately while the robot cell is developed on its own.

Place the CNC mill and outgoing conveyor provisionally. Their first positions
do not need to be final. Leave enough room to open and access the CNC door, and
provide clearance for the gripper, workpiece, and approach and retract motions.

The final cell layout is your design decision, and there is no prescribed
arrangement. Among the choices are the relative positions and orientations of
the robot, conveyors, CNC mill, and access areas. For example, the
conveyors could be arranged in line or at an angle, and the CNC mill could be
placed beside the robot or across from the conveyors. These are only starting
points; you may develop another arrangement that gives a good combination of
robot reach, clear motion paths, material flow, and access to the equipment.

### Check reachability and clearance

The [VC reachability overview](visual_components.qmd#sec-vc-robot-analysis)
explains how workspace profiles, jogging, joint checks, and collision detection
complement one another.

Use the robot's `WorkSpace2D` or `WorkSpace3D` component properties to display its
approximate workspace, also called its work envelope. Use this envelope as
rough guidance for the initial cell layout and for estimating basic distances
between the robot, conveyors, and CNC mill. @fig-agilus-workspace shows the
`WorkSpace2D` profile around the Agilus robot used in this project. The linked
VC overview contains the relevant Academy lessons.

This profile approximates position reach; it does not prove that the robot can
achieve the required tool orientation at every point. The distinction between
[reachable and dexterous workspace](kinematics.qmd#sec-workspace-types) explains
why checking the complete task poses is necessary.

![The approximate `WorkSpace2D` profile of the KUKA KR6 R900 Agilus displayed in Visual Components.](<img/VC Components Previews/agilus_2D_workspace.png>){#fig-agilus-workspace width=90% fig-alt="A KUKA KR6 R900 Agilus in Visual Components surrounded by the outline of its two-dimensional workspace profile."}

For more detailed and reliable tuning of the arrangement, mount the gripper
(see @sec-mount-gripper for how to mount and use it), generate one grey
cylinder, and grip it. Then use the **Jog** tool to move the complete robot,
tool, and workpiece assembly through the important task poses.
After all, it is the workpiece that must be placed at the positions and
orientations required by the task. The cell must therefore allow the robot to
move the workpiece through these poses without exceeding joint limits,
approaching singularities, or colliding with the surrounding equipment. While
jogging, use the [**Jog** panel](https://help.visualcomponents.com/5.0/Premium/en/English/Robot%20Programming/Jog_panel.htm)
to monitor each joint's current value and permitted range. This shows when a
target pose pushes one or more joints toward their limits. Enable **Color
Highlight** in the **Limits** group to also mark
the affected robot geometry in red when a joint limit is exceeded. Enable a
[collision detector](https://help.visualcomponents.com/5.0/Premium/en/English/Robot%20Programming/Other%20Operations/Detecting_collisions.htm)
and start the simulation once to initialize it. You can
then reset the simulation and use the detector while jogging; collisions with
the CNC, conveyors, pedestal, and other equipment are highlighted in yellow in the 3D
view. 

Manual jogging checks individual poses but does not validate every point along
the programmed motion between them. After teaching representative motions, run
the program with collision detection and the
[**Limits** tools](https://help.visualcomponents.com/5.0/Premium/en/English/Robot%20Programming/Other%20Operations/Limiting_a_robot_and_its_joints.htm)
enabled, including the singularity check.

Before teaching the complete program, verify that:

- the robot can reach the pickup, CNC loading, outgoing conveyor, and home poses,
- the gripper and workpiece fit through the CNC opening,
- the robot can approach and retract without crossing the machine or fence,
- the conveyor sensor is located at a repeatable pickup pose.

These checks are easier to correct before many robot positions depend on the
layout.

### Consider safety while the layout develops

Do not wait until the end of the project to think about safety, but also do not
spend time drawing final fencing while the equipment is still moving between
tests. During layout design, consider where people need access for loading,
teaching, clearing faults, and maintenance; where parts and people could enter
the cell intentionally or unintentionally; where a gate could be placed; and
whether robot motion creates trapping points against the CNC mill, fence, or
other fixed equipment.

Once the equipment positions are mostly stable and the relevant robot motions
have been checked, use the **Fence and Wall Builder** from `Facilities -
Factory` to draw the perimeter caging. This is usually the most convenient way
to create and revise the fence. Simulation does not replace a risk assessment,
but it makes alternative layouts easier to examine before positions and
control logic become difficult to change. The safety process and the priority
given to reducing hazards through design are discussed in the
[risk-assessment process](robot_safety.qmd#sec-risk-assessment) and the
[risk-reduction priorities](robot_safety.qmd#sec-risk-reduction) on the robot
safety page.

After placing the cell equipment, select the newly added components and use
**Move to Layout** to assign them to the `Robot cell` sublayout. Check the
**Layouts** tab afterwards to make sure that no cell component remains at the
`ROOT` level. Moving the components together is usually quicker than assigning
each component immediately after adding it.

## Mount and configure the gripper {#sec-mount-gripper}

Mount the **Generic 3 Finger Gripper** directly on the robot flange using
**PnP**. Move the gripper toward the flange until the compatible physical
interfaces are highlighted, then continue moving it until the components snap
together. This physical connection makes the gripper follow the flange when
the robot is jogged. The **Add a robot tool** chapter in the
[Introduction to Robot Teaching](https://academy.visualcomponents.com/lessons/introduction-to-robot-teaching/)
video demonstrates this workflow.

Enable automatic I/O connection when mounting the gripper. This option is
enabled by default and avoids having to connect the gripper's input and output
signals to the robot manually.

Before configuring these signals, it is important to understand how standard
grasping works in VC. A grasp action searches for products inside a detection
volume around a selected tool frame. When a product is found, VC fixes its pose
relative to that frame, so the product moves with the robot. A release action
removes this logical attachment. Physical finger contact is not calculated,
which is why VC can grasp a product even when no gripper model is mounted or
the fingers do not touch it. VC also provides rigid-body physics for custom
contact-based simulations, but that is a separate, more complex approach and
is not used in this project.

The finger animation is therefore not what holds the product in the standard
simulation, but it is still important. Realistic open and closed widths let you
check the gripper's geometric capacity and its clearance around the workpiece.
They also make collision checking more meaningful because an open gripper
occupies a different volume from a closed one. Visible finger motion helps you
understand and debug the program sequence, and it makes the simulation clearer
and more convincing in customer or sales presentations. It does not validate
real gripping force, payload capacity, deformation, or slip.

The general relationship between robot I/O ports, component signals, and
**Actions Configuration** is introduced in
[Robot I/O and signal actions](visual_components.qmd#sec-vc-robot-io). The
configuration below applies those mechanisms specifically to the project
gripper.

The logical grasp and release actions are configured in the robot's **Actions
Configuration** properties. In most VC robot components, outputs `1` to `16`
are predefined for grasping and releasing with the default tool frames. These
outputs can be used for a tool without movable joints, such as a suction cup,
or even without a visible gripper. In that case, the output does not need to be
connected to another component: setting it only triggers the robot's internal
grasp or release action. Always inspect the selected robot's mappings because
component models can differ.

A gripper with movable fingers requires both parts of the simulation. The robot
output must trigger VC's internal grasp or release action and drive the gripper
joint so that the fingers close or open. After mounting the gripper, inspect its
**Control** properties and the robot's signal connections. Automatically
connected custom gripper I/O commonly starts at robot port `100`.

In the tested cell, robot output `100` is connected to the gripper input
`IN_J1_Action`: `TRUE` closes the fingers and `FALSE` opens them. Configure the
same output in **Actions Configuration** so that `TRUE` also performs **Grasp**
and `FALSE` performs **Release**. Select a tool frame at the centre of the
gripping region and set a detection volume that contains the cylinder at the
grasp pose without including nearby products. It is usually easiest to align
one of the robot's native tool frames with the gripper's TCP after mounting the
gripper, and then use that frame for both the grasp action and the robot motion
statements. @fig-gripper-action-config shows the signal connection and action
configuration together. @sec-cell-tcp explains the TCP setup in more detail.

![Robot output `100` is connected to the movable gripper and configured to perform the internal VC grasp and release actions using `Tool_TCP`.](<img/VC Components Previews/agilus_gripper_action_config.png>){#fig-gripper-action-config width=100% fig-alt="Visual Components showing a KUKA robot with a three-jaw gripper, the signal connections between robot output 100 and the gripper, and Actions Configuration set to Grasp on true and Release on false using Tool TCP."}

Opening and closing the gripper takes time. After commanding it, read its
separate open-state or closed-state feedback and wait until the requested state
has been reached before moving the robot. The **Test the signals** chapter in
the [Model a robot gripper, part II](https://academy.visualcomponents.com/lessons/model-a-robot-gripper-part-ii/)
lesson demonstrates this I/O and feedback workflow.

Finally, use VC's measure tool to determine the cylinder size and set the
gripper's `J1_OpenValue` and `J1_CloseValue` properties accordingly. Run the
sequence and confirm that the fingers fully clear the cylinder when open and
close to a realistic gripping width.

## Define and select the TCP {#sec-cell-tcp}

The attached gripper contributes a TCP frame. Select a frame located at the
centre of the gripping region and use it as the active tool frame in the robot
motion statements. Inspect its position and orientation rather than assuming
that the component's default frame is suitable. If necessary, move one of the
robot's native tool frames to the required TCP and use that frame consistently
throughout the program.

The frame should be located and oriented according to the physical task, not
only at a convenient point in the 3D model. Review [frames and
poses](frames_poses.qmd) if the TCP or reference-frame behavior is unclear.

## CNC mill

Use the **Process Machine - CNC** component. Configure a short process time
during development and inspect its command and feedback signals:

| CNC signal | Direction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM_PLC_OpenDoor` | Into CNC | Request the door to open. |
| `FROM_PLC_CloseDoor` | Into CNC | Request the door to close. |
| `FROM_PLC_StartProcess` | Into CNC | Start the machining process. |
| `TO_PLC_DoorsOpen` | From CNC | Door-open feedback. |
| `TO_PLC_DoorsClosed` | From CNC | Door-closed feedback. |
| `TO_PLC_ProcessIsRunning` | From CNC | Machining is currently running. |

There is no separate process-complete signal in this model. The controller must
first observe `ProcessIsRunning = TRUE` and then wait for it to return to
`FALSE`. Waiting only for `FALSE` could incorrectly report completion before
the process has started.

# Stage 1: internal VC control {#sec-cell-internal-control}

The general workflows for creating robot motions and organizing a VC robot
program are introduced in
[Jogging and teaching motion](visual_components.qmd#sec-vc-robot-teaching) and
[Program structure and logic](visual_components.qmd#sec-vc-robot-programs).
Apply them here to build the project-specific sequence.

Connect the pickup sensor and CNC signals to available robot input and output
ports. The robot program is now responsible for the complete cell: it waits for
a part, operates the CNC, and performs all robot and gripper motions.

During this stage, the detected part must remain at the taught pickup pose. The
simplest option is to configure the Conveyor Sensor to **StopPart** when it
detects a product. Alternatively, route the sensor signal so that detection
sets the incoming conveyor's `PowerOn` signal to `FALSE`. This alternative
requires an inverted signal or equivalent routing logic; connecting a sensor
whose active value is `TRUE` directly to `PowerOn` would have the opposite effect. In either
case, verify that the part stops before teaching the pickup pose and that the
conveyor does not restart while the robot is gripping it.

## Use meaningful subroutines

Do not write the complete task as one long `Main` routine. At minimum, organize
the motions into operations corresponding to:

- picking a part from the conveyor,
- moving to and loading the CNC,
- running the CNC process,
- unloading the CNC and placing the finished part, and
- returning home.

Choose names that describe what each operation achieves. Each routine should
start and finish in a predictable situation and contain the details tightly
coupled to that operation. For example, the pick routine should operate the
gripper and verify its feedback before retracting.

The internal `Main` routine should read like the material flow rather than a
list of individual robot motions. This makes the program easier to test now and
provides subroutines that can be requested by the PLC later.

## Validate before continuing

Run repeated complete cycles and verify:

- all robot positions and configurations are reachable,
- approach and retract paths do not collide,
- the correct base and tool frames are active,
- the gripper reaches its commanded state before the next motion,
- the part is attached and released at the expected points,
- the CNC door and process sequence completes correctly, and
- the robot ends each cycle at a known home pose.

Do not proceed to external PLC control until this version works reliably.

## Moving equipment after teaching positions

If you must relocate or rotate the robot after teaching positions, change
**Lock Positions** from **To reference** to **To World** before moving it. Change
the setting back afterwards. This holds the taught poses fixed in the world
while the robot base moves.

For equipment-relative tasks, consider defining robot base frames on the
relevant equipment instead. A pose defined relative to a CNC fixture then moves
with that fixture, which can make later layout changes easier. Choose the method
that reflects which physical relationship should remain fixed.

## Integrate the conveyor and robot-cell sublayouts {#sec-cell-integrate}

After the internally controlled robot program works reliably with the temporary
feeder, connect the two subsystems. Disconnect or remove the robot cell's feeder,
move the `Conveyor system` and `Robot cell` sublayouts together, and connect the
appropriate conveyor paths. Start the original mixed feeder in the `Conveyor
system` sublayout only after this connection is working.

Run the complete material flow again before adding PLC control. Check not only
whether the robot cycle still runs, but also whether parts queue at the expected
locations, whether upstream conveyors become blocked, and whether the timing
between part arrival, conveyor stopping, and robot pickup remains reliable.

# Stage 2: external PLC control {#sec-cell-external-control}

The distinction between VC-internal signals and values mapped to an external
PLC is introduced in
[Internal VC control and external PLC control](visual_components.qmd#sec-vc-external-control).
The following sections define the project-specific control boundary and
interface.

The final system separates cell coordination from robot motion. Sensors and
machine actuators are mapped to CODESYS, while the PLC and robot exchange
high-level operation commands and status values.

| Controller | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| PLC | Run and stop control for the ordinary conveyors, pickup-sensor evaluation, CNC door and process control, and overall operation order. Product routing and the complete pusher transfer remain internal to VC; timeout and fault handling are optional extensions. |
| Robot program | Robot motion, approach and retract paths, gripper actions, and gripper feedback within each requested operation. |

The gripper remains under robot control because its actions are tightly coupled
to the pick and place motions. The PLC sequence controls the ordinary conveyor
run command and CNC equipment, while the Pusher Conveyor retains its internal
routing and transfer behavior.

Remove the direct conveyor-sensor and CNC connections from the active robot
program. Retain the local robot-to-gripper connections. Keep the internally
controlled routine as a tested reference while developing a separate
PLC-controlled main routine.

## Two interacting state machines

A useful way to structure the control is to use a state machine on each side,
but at different levels:

- The **PLC FSM** represents progress through the complete material flow and
  decides which device may act next.
- The **robot-side FSM** accepts one operation request, executes the
  selected robot subroutine, and reports its status.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    PLC[PLC cell FSM]
    ROBOT[VC robot FSM]
    CONVEYOR[Ordinary conveyors and pickup sensor]
    CNC[CNC mill]
    ROUTINES[Robot subroutines]

    PLC -->|Command| ROBOT
    ROBOT -->|State and active command| PLC
    PLC -->|Run| CONVEYOR
    CONVEYOR -->|Part detected| PLC
    PLC -->|Door and process commands| CNC
    CNC -->|Door and process feedback| PLC
    ROBOT -->|Call operation| ROUTINES
```

The PLC must not calculate robot joint motion, and the robot must not silently
continue the complete production sequence after one requested operation. Both
controllers should be understandable and testable independently.

## Robot command properties {#sec-cell-command-interface}

On the VC **Modeling** tab, add three integer properties to the robot component.
Place them in a group named `PLC`:

| Property | Direction | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `PLC::Command` | PLC to robot | Requested operation; zero means no command. |
| `PLC::RobotState` | Robot to PLC | State of the robot command interface. |
| `PLC::ActiveCommand` | Robot to PLC | Command accepted and currently being handled. |

`PLC` is only the property-group name. In a robot-program expression, the `::`
syntax separates the group and property names.

Use the following interface contract:

| Command | Required robot operation |
|---:|---|
| `0` | No command or PLC acknowledgement |
| `1` | Pick the part from the conveyor |
| `2` | Load the CNC |
| `3` | Unload the CNC and place the part on the conveyor |
| `4` | Move to the home pose |

| Robot state | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| `0` | Initializing |
| `1` | Ready for a command |
| `2` | Busy executing the accepted command |
| `3` | Command completed and waiting for acknowledgement |
| `4` | Invalid command or fault |

The robot program must use `PLC::ActiveCommand` to choose the required
subroutine. You can implement this selection with `If` and `Else` statements or
with a `Switch Case`. `Switch Case` is often compact and easy to read when each
integer command corresponds to one operation.

## Required command handshake

For every robot operation:

1. The PLC waits for robot state `Ready`.
2. The PLC writes and holds the requested command.
3. The robot copies it to `ActiveCommand` and reports `Busy`.
4. The PLC verifies that the intended command was accepted.
5. The robot executes the complete subroutine and reports `Done`.
6. The PLC clears `Command` to `0` as acknowledgement.
7. The robot clears `ActiveCommand` and returns to `Ready`.

This level-based handshake is preferable to short pulses because a pulse could
be missed between an OPC UA update and a PLC scan.

::: {.callout-tip}
VC robot programs provide a dedicated wait statement only for binary robot
inputs. To wait for an integer component property, use a `While` loop with a
short delay, for example `0.05 s`. The loop condition should describe when the
program must continue waiting. The delay prevents an empty polling loop from
consuming simulation execution time.
:::

# OPC UA interface

The [PLC-integration and virtual-commissioning section](simulation.qmd#sec-virtual-commissioning)
explains the complete signal path and provides the relevant VC Academy setup
lesson.

Expose the required CODESYS variables through **Symbol Configuration** and
connect VC to the CODESYS OPC UA server. With CODESYS Control Win SL on the same
computer, the server address is normally:

```text
opc.tcp://localhost:4840
```

VC acts as the OPC UA client. Use separate Connectivity variable groups for
values sent in each direction.

| PLC variable | VC property or signal | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| `iRobotCommand` | `PLC::Command` | PLC to VC |
| `xConveyorRun` | Shared `PowerOnSignal` for the ordinary conveyors | PLC to VC |
| `xCncOpenDoor` | `FROM_PLC_OpenDoor` | PLC to VC |
| `xCncCloseDoor` | `FROM_PLC_CloseDoor` | PLC to VC |
| `xCncStartProcess` | `FROM_PLC_StartProcess` | PLC to VC |
| `PLC::RobotState` | `iRobotState` | VC to PLC |
| `PLC::ActiveCommand` | `iRobotActiveCommand` | VC to PLC |
| Pickup sensor | `xPartAtPick` | VC to PLC |
| `TO_PLC_DoorsOpen` | `xCncDoorOpen` | VC to PLC |
| `TO_PLC_DoorsClosed` | `xCncDoorClosed` | VC to PLC |
| `TO_PLC_ProcessIsRunning` | `xCncProcessRunning` | VC to PLC |

If you retained the sensor's internal **StopPart** action from Stage 1, it can
continue to hold the product at the exact taught pose despite communication
delay. The PLC must still turn off the conveyor when it receives `xPartAtPick`,
preventing the conveyor and following products from continuing. Document the
internal stop as a simulation convenience rather than PLC behavior.

# Commissioning procedure

Test the connected system incrementally:

1. Start CODESYS Control Win SL and run the PLC application with production
   disabled and `iRobotCommand = 0`.
2. Connect both OPC UA variable groups in VC.
3. Reset and start the VC simulation.
4. Confirm that the robot initializes, moves home, and reports `Ready`.
5. Test each robot command and its complete handshake individually.
6. Test the conveyor sensor and each CNC command and feedback pair.
7. Enable production and run the complete PLC-controlled cycle.

Monitor the PLC FSM state, robot command, robot state, active command, pickup
sensor, conveyor output, CNC door feedback, and process-running feedback. When
the system stops, first identify which controller and state is waiting, then
check the condition required to leave that state.

# Requirements and deliverables

Your submission shall include:

- the VC layout with functional geometry, configured tool and signals,
- the internally controlled robot program used for initial validation,
- the PLC-controlled robot program and meaningful motion subroutines,
- the CODESYS PLC program,
- an I/O list showing every OPC UA variable and its direction,
- diagrams or tables documenting the PLC and robot state machines, and
- evidence that the internal and externally controlled cycles were tested.

The externally controlled solution shall satisfy these acceptance criteria:

- the PLC, not the robot, coordinates ordinary conveyor motion and the CNC,
- the Pusher Conveyor retains its tested internal routing and transfer behavior,
- the robot accepts only defined operation commands,
- every command follows the specified acknowledgement handshake,
- robot commands are held until acknowledged rather than sent as short pulses,
- the CNC process is confirmed to start before completion is evaluated,
- disabling production prevents another cycle without interrupting an active
  robot or CNC operation,
- the robot and gripper finish each requested operation in a predictable state,
  and
- the complete material flow repeats without manual intervention.

Develop the normal sequence first. Timeouts and fault recovery are optional
extensions and should be added only after the nominal cycle and communication
interface are stable.
